text:
By William Bitibiri
Only three managers have won the league with Manchester United. Paul Scholes and Nicky Butt knew two. Ernest Mangnall was the name that stopped them.
“Who!?”
“Never heard of him,” Butt said.
Scholes was equally puzzled. Mangnall won United’s first two league titles, in 1907-08 and 1910-11. Sir Matt Busby added five, Sir Alex Ferguson 13.
“F****** hell,” Scholes replied.

It is an understandable reaction. More than a century on, Mangnall’s achievements have faded from the conversation around United’s greatest managers. His two titles are often overlooked beside the five won by Busby and the 13 delivered by Ferguson.
But the numbers tell an unusual story. United have won 20 league titles under just three managers. Liverpool have also won 20, but theirs have been shared between six: Bill Shankly, Bob Paisley, Joe Fagan, Kenny Dalglish, Jurgen Klopp and Arne Slot.
Busby and Ferguson account for 18 of United’s 20. Their influence went beyond trophies. They shaped teams, set standards and helped define the club’s identity.
That raises a question beyond the familiar search for Ferguson’s successor. Have United become so accustomed to the leadership of two extraordinary individuals that it struggles to imagine success without one?
The messiah came, then United waited 17 years for the second coming. United are now praying for a third.
The foundations
When Matt Busby arrived at Manchester United in 1945, the club was far from the institution we recognise today.
Old Trafford had been badly damaged during the Second World War and was unusable.
United were playing their home games at Maine Road, sharing Manchester City's ground while trying to recover from the financial and physical consequences of the war.
Busby had played for Manchester City and Liverpool, and had been offered the chance to manage the latter before taking the job at United. There was little in his background to suggest he would become the defining figure in the history of either club, let alone the man who would lay the foundations for modern Manchester United.
He arrived with a clear idea of what he wanted. Busby wanted to build something that would last. Young players needed a route into the first team, United had to play with ambition and the club should compete with the best in Europe.
His relationship with youth was particularly important. The Busby Babes became more than a football team. They represented an idea: that United could produce its own players, develop them and trust them to carry the club forward.
Munich threatened to destroy everything. Eight United players lost their lives in the air disaster of 1958, alongside other members of the travelling party. Busby was seriously injured. The tragedy could have ended the club's ambitions, but instead became part of the story of its eventual resurrection.
He rebuilt. George Best, Denis Law and Bobby Charlton helped take United back to the top. In 1968, they beat Benfica 4-1 at Wembley to win the European Cup, becoming the first English club to lift the trophy 10 years on from the tragedy.
For Aaron Burns, a former United academy player who now leads the Association of Former Manchester United Players, the significance of that history is still felt inside the club.
“Manchester United is aspiration and inspiration,” he told me.
“You walk into the building, you see the legends, but you also see the heartache. You see the Munich disaster, which is remembered and talked about all the time.”
Burns remembers being a young boy at Carrington, suddenly finding himself in the company of players he had previously only watched on television. Roy Keane and Ruud van Nistelrooy were around the training ground. Ferguson was there, too.
“You'd bump into Sir Alex and you're probably walking in ones or twos. And then he’d just stop you and be like, 'Aaron, how's your grandma?'”
Those encounters left an impression. History wasn’t just in pictures on walls; it was living, breathing, carried in the testimony of people who worked there, many of whom had witnessed different eras of the club.
Burns sees a direct connection between the two great managerial reigns.
“Ferguson built some core values, but he built it on top of Sir Matt Busby's principles,” he said.
“You build on top of, not next to.”
Ferguson inherited a club with an established identity, but he did not spend his time trying to recreate Busby's teams. He took the foundations and made them his own.
Busby's departure, however, was not followed by an immediate continuation of his success. Wilf McGuinness, Frank O'Farrell, Tommy Docherty, Dave Sexton and Ron Atkinson all took charge before Ferguson arrived.
They won four major domestic cups between them, but no league title.
United would not be champions again until 1993.
The man from Govan
Alex Ferguson was born in Govan, Glasgow, less than 20 miles from Busby's birthplace in Orbiston, Bellshill.
There were obvious parallels between them. Both came from working-class Scottish backgrounds, valued youth development and attacking football, and saw management as more than picking a team on a Saturday afternoon.
Ferguson's route to Old Trafford was different, though. By the time he arrived in November 1986, his achievements at Aberdeen had established him as one of Britain's most respected managers. Beating Real Madrid in the 1983 European Cup Winners' Cup final had announced him on the European stage.
He was not walking into a club ready to dominate. United had not won the league since 1967 and were still living in the shadow of Liverpool's success.
Ferguson had to change the habits of the club before he could change its fortunes.
There was no instant transformation. The FA Cup arrived in 1990, followed by the European Cup Winners' Cup in 1991. The league title finally came in 1993, ending a 26-year wait.
By then, Ferguson had begun building something that would dominate English football for the next two decades.
The Class of '92 became the most obvious symbol of that work. David Beckham, Scholes, Butt, Gary Neville, Phil Neville and Ryan Giggs represented a system that gave young players a route into the first team and expected them to take responsibility when they got there.
Ferguson also understood that a successful team could not stand still. He rebuilt it repeatedly, moving on established players and bringing in new ones without allowing the standards to drop. The treble in 1999 was the high point of one generation. The title-winning teams of the mid-2000s and the side that won the Champions League in 2008 were built around another.
Gary Neville's autobiography, Red, offers a glimpse of how that culture operated from inside the dressing room.
Recalling United's comeback at Newcastle in March 1996, Neville describes how United overturned a 2-0 half-time deficit to win 3-2, with Eric Cantona scoring the winner.
“That second half was an occasion when I felt the Manchester United spirit course through the team,” he wrote.
“It relies on excellence from individuals – from Schmeichel and Bruce, who were immense that evening, and from Eric, who popped up to score the winner – but there is also something collective.
“It's unspoken but unmistakable: let's get this match won. It's our time.”
The word that stands out is collective. Ferguson's United were full of outstanding individuals, but everyone was expected to contribute to the team's cause.
Roy Keane's The Second Half provides another view of the dressing room. Keane describes a group in which senior players helped one another, particularly when new arrivals were struggling to settle.
He recalls the support given to Diego Forlan, who joined from Independiente in 2002 and scored just 17 goals in 98 appearances during his United spell.
“If a player tried – and Diego did – we'd drag him with us; we'd try and help him,” Keane wrote.
It was not the manager's job alone to maintain the standards. The players were expected to take responsibility for the environment around them.
Ferguson made that expectation clear.
In Leading, he wrote: “The minute that we don't work harder than the other team, we'll not be Manchester United.”
Talent mattered, but so did drive, resilience and a refusal to accept that the job was done. Ferguson's teams had to earn their reputation every time they went out.
Neville has also explained what made Ferguson so effective. He pointed to the difficult conversations he was prepared to have with his players.
“If you were left out from one game to the next, he spoke to each individual player every game.”
That personal contact was matched by a willingness to trust the people around him. Ferguson allowed his assistants to lead training and his medical staff to manage their work, rather than involving himself in every detail.
“Now you imagine two things: one about the trust that builds in your team, which is very rare. But secondly, when he actually spoke on match day and he came alive, his words meant a lot. So his words were quite rare.”
What does success actually mean?
Paul Scholes has a straightforward answer.
“Win the league,” he told me.
“A successful Manchester United manager, he's got to win the Premier League.”
He does not believe winning a cup competition is enough to define a successful United manager.
Plenty of clubs can win a cup. The real test, in his view, is whether a manager can build a team capable of challenging for the league.
“Success was winning a trophy every season.”
Wayne Barton, Author and Manchester United Historian
“I haven't felt since Sir Alex went that we've actually got a team to win the league,” Scholes added.
That is the standard Ferguson left behind, but it raises a wider question: is winning the Premier League the only measure of success at Manchester United?
If the only measure is a league title, the answer is simple. Only Busby, Ferguson and Mangnall have achieved it.
But football is not always that straightforward. Ron Atkinson won two FA Cups in the 1980s. Louis van Gaal won the FA Cup. Jose Mourinho delivered the League Cup and Europa League in the same season. Erik ten Hag won the League Cup and FA Cup.
Are those managers failures?
Wayne Barton, an esteemed historian of Manchester United and author of several books on the club, is reluctant to make the judgement quite so simply.
“I think in the modern era, it means what the modern era definition of Manchester United manager success is: winning the league,” he told me.
“I think that's the minimum.”
But Barton makes a distinction between the expectation at United and his own definition of success.
“You can't always win the league, but you're second in the league. If your team is in a cup final every season or two cup finals, or competing for the league, I think that is what I would determine as success for a United manager.”
Barton also pointed to Ferguson's own interpretation of the job:
“I think this was Alex Ferguson's interpretation of it: success was winning a trophy every season.”
Winning a trophy is one thing; building a team that can dominate an era is another. The question is whether the club's identity and standards can survive beyond the manager who delivers it.
“I haven’t felt since Sir Alex went that we’ve actually got a team to win the league.”
Paul Scholes, former Man Utd midfielder
“Manchester United is a different beast, but you have to embrace the pressure.”
Nicky Butt, former Man Utd midfielder
“Since Sir Alex left, they have had a leadership problem.”
Ralf Rangnick, former Man Utd interim boss
'The United way'
Ask supporters what makes Manchester United different and the answers tend to be familiar: attacking football, young players, courage, entertainment, standards.
But how much of that identity belongs to the club itself, and how much belongs to the men who created it?
Rob Smyth, the journalist and author, believes Busby and Ferguson occupied a position at Manchester United that no manager has come close to matching since.
Smyth said no United manager since has risen to the same level as a singular figure in English football.
He described the different ways in which the pair came to be regarded almost as gods at Old Trafford.
“Busby was seen as a god because he was untouchable; you couldn't connect with him. Ferguson was seen as a god because he was so successful, and you couldn't wrong him, otherwise, you were out.”
Smyth believes Ferguson's relationship with United's history was particularly important. He did not see himself as bigger than the club, but as someone serving something larger.
“Ferguson understood it from day one. He understood that he was a custodian of what Busby built,” Smyth said.
“He was subservient to the idea that Manchester United is something bigger than himself. But he was serving the club.”
There is a contrast with clubs such as Ajax and Barcelona, where a recognisable footballing philosophy has been embedded into the wider structure. At United, the identity has often felt more closely tied to the manager.
Burns agrees that the club's DNA is difficult to define.
“It's got its own DNA,” he said.
“It's just a little bit less explainable than Ajax and the Cruyff method or Real Madrid and the Galacticos. It's harder to digest and compartmentalise.”
For Burns, the answer lies in standards and connectivity. The club must feel connected from the academy to the first team, and players must believe there is a genuine pathway if they are good enough.
Butt made a similar point when I asked him what makes a successful Manchester United manager.
“I think there are two or three things that are success. It's obviously winning in the right way, upholding the standards of the club,” he said. “But for me, what makes a successful Manchester United manager is connectivity.”
He was talking about more than the relationship between a manager and his players. The entire club needs to pull in the same direction, from the academy to the first team and the people working behind the scenes.
“Connectivity throughout the club with the people that work there on a day-to-day basis,” he said. “They're just as important as the first-team players.”
He believes the academy remains the bloodline of United. There needs to be a visible route from the younger age groups into the senior side, with players given the opportunity to make the step up if they are good enough.
“There needs to be an opportunity for someone to come in at under nine and be in the first team in nine years and see that pathway at every single moment,” he said.
It is a point that goes beyond the familiar celebration of United's academy record. The club has named at least one academy graduate in every matchday squad since October 1937. Butt believes United has sometimes become fragmented, with different departments operating separately.
“It has to be connected and cohesive throughout the whole building,” he said.
“And there has to be the feeling that if you're good enough, you're going to get the opportunity to play.”
Busby and Ferguson both understood the importance of youth. But they also had the authority to make their ideas happen.
Their successors have inherited the expectation without necessarily inheriting the same power.
The succession problem
Ferguson knew replacing him would be an enormous challenge.
In Leading, he was candid about the search for his successor.
“At United we didn't have an obvious internal successor, though it was not for want of trying,” he wrote.
He had encouraged Ryan Giggs, Gary Neville, Darren Fletcher, Nicky Butt, Dwight Yorke and Andy Cole to earn their coaching credentials. But he did not believe a player should move straight from the dressing room into the manager's office.
“United tried that once when Wilf McGuinness succeeded Matt Busby in 1969,” Ferguson wrote. “It was a disaster.”
He also revealed that he had admired Pep Guardiola and asked him to phone before accepting an offer from another club. Guardiola eventually joined Bayern Munich in July 2013.
Other candidates were unavailable. Jose Mourinho had given his word to Roman Abramovich that he would return to Chelsea, Carlo Ancelotti was heading to Real Madrid, Jurgen Klopp was staying at Borussia Dortmund and Louis van Gaal was preparing to lead the Netherlands at the World Cup.
Eventually, United chose David Moyes.
Ferguson defended the appointment in his book, pointing to Moyes' work at Everton and the financial constraints under which he had operated.
“Sadly, things did not turn out for David as he and we all wished,” he wrote.
He also acknowledged that the transition could have been handled differently, suggesting that keeping Mike Phelan might have helped Moyes navigate the many layers of the club.
But the transition was bigger than the appointment itself. Ferguson retired. Chief executive David Gill left. The manager who had controlled the club for 26 years was gone, alongside a key figure who had helped him run it.
Danny Taylor, who covered United during Ferguson's reign, remembers just how much of the club's operation revolved around the manager.
After United won the Champions League in 1999, Ferguson held a press conference for local Manchester beat journalists rather than the wider press. It was a small example of the control he exercised, even over details that might seem relatively minor.
Taylor experienced the more difficult side of that relationship, too. After writing a book covering United's turbulent 2005-06 season, he was banned from Ferguson's Friday press conferences from 2007 until the manager retired in 2013.
He had not had an argument with Ferguson.
“He used to always say, 'I really encourage young people',” Taylor told me.
“But the journalists, he thought we were all babies, he thought we were all kids.”
Taylor recalled a colleague's first encounter with Ferguson, after which the manager reportedly remarked that he “looks like the bass player of Oasis”.
It is an amusing recollection, but Taylor's wider point is more serious. Ferguson was fiercely protective of his territory and maintained a tight grip on the club's operation.
“You just thought, when he leaves, the club is just very, very ill-equipped at all levels to deal with what's next,” Taylor said.
The reality is that the authority Busby and Ferguson exercised was part of their success, but it left a vacuum when they went.
Moyes himself later reflected on the difficulty of the job in 2014.
“I was devastated to lose the job because it was something I felt we could make a real success of,” he said.
“In the end, I don't feel I was given the time to succeed or fail.”
He also pointed to the fact that both he and former executive vice-chairman Ed Woodward were new to their roles.
“I had taken over from the most successful manager in history,” Moyes said.
“The chief executive had taken over from one of the most renowned administrators in the game. So it was a new job for two people.”
Roy Keane was less sympathetic towards the players who failed to help Moyes.
In The Second Half, Keane questioned the strength of the dressing room and the responsibility of players to support a new manager.
“Not liking a manager, for whatever reason, can never be an excuse for not going out and doing your best,” he wrote.
His conclusion was damning: “Looking at what happened to David Moyes, I have to conclude that he can't have had a strong dressing room; he had a weak dressing room.”
The failure of the post-Ferguson era cannot be attributed to the manager alone. The players, the owners, the board and the wider structure all had a role in what followed.
Moyes was the first, but certainly not the last.
Ryan Giggs took charge on an interim basis after Moyes' dismissal, before Louis van Gaal arrived in 2014.
The Dutchman brought a clear yet alien philosophy and delivered the FA Cup, but could not restore United to the top of the league.
Jose Mourinho followed, winning the League Cup and Europa League and finishing second

מנצ'סטר יונייטד מחזיקה ב-20 אליפויות ליגה, אך נתון מפתיע חושף כי 18 מתוכן הושגו תחת שני מנג'רים בלבד בהיסטוריה הארוכה של המועדון - סר מאט באזבי וסר אלכס פרגוסון. שאר האליפויות מתחלקות בין אליפות אחת של ארנסט מנגנל בתחילת המאה ה-20, בעוד שורה של מנג'רים אחרים לא הצליחו לזכות בתואר הנכסף.

באזבי ופרגוסון לא רק זכו בתארים אלא עיצבו את הזהות של המועדון, שילבו שחקני צעירים והניחו יסודות עמוקים שהפכו את המועדון לאימפריה עולמית. הצלחתם חסרת התקדים יצרה רף ציפיות גבוה במיוחד, המקשה על כל מאמן שמגיע אחריהם לשחזר את הצלחתם ולשמור על יציבות לאורך זמן.
